description: This policy brief examines Iran’s emerging overland supply architecture under sustained maritime constraint. It argues that Iran’s logistics adaptation is moving beyond discrete alternative corridors toward a functionally differentiated rail–road system linking Chinese gateways, Central Asian transit networks, Iranian border crossings, and domestic distribution. Rail and trucking are treated as complementary rather than interchangeable modes: rail supports scheduled, containerized, heavier-volume flows, while trucking adds flexibility for urgent, high-value, smaller-lot, and final-distribution cargo. The brief analyzes China–Central Asia rail data, Horgos and Alashankou gateway patterns, China–Iran block-train services, TIR and trucking evidence, APRIN Dry Port specifications, and reported Iranian border, fuel, and driver constraints. It concludes that the central issue is capacity conversion: overland resilience depends on how much nominal gateway and corridor access becomes reliable delivered supply inside Iran, not on route count alone.
abstract: This policy brief examines Iran’s emerging overland supply architecture under sustained maritime constraint. It argues that Iran’s logistics adaptation is moving beyond discrete alternative corridors toward a functionally differentiated rail–road system linking Chinese gateways, Central Asian transit networks, Iranian border crossings, and domestic distribution. Rail and trucking are complementary rather than interchangeable modes: rail supports scheduled, containerized, heavier-volume flows, while trucking adds flexibility for urgent, high-value, smaller-lot, fragmented, project, and final-distribution cargo. The analysis combines official railway and border statistics, published facility capacity, current reporting on route use and disruption, and commercial logistics materials used only to identify marketed service characteristics. It finds that China–Central Asia rail data show moderate, not indiscriminate, expansion; Horgos provides the stronger westbound gateway signal; and TIR and operator evidence indicate growing commercial readiness while also showing that advertised “direct” services can include transloading. The brief concludes that Iran’s overland system has become more operationally mature and commercially differentiated, but its strategic role remains threshold delay and selective continuity rather than maritime-scale substitution. The central issue is capacity conversion: resilience depends on how much nominal gateway and corridor access becomes reliable delivered supply inside Iran.

methodology.framework_name: Capacity Conversion and Rail–Road Overland Supply Resilience Framework
methodology.source_basis: Exploratory policy assessment combining official railway and border statistics, published facility capacity, reporting on route use and disruption, and commercial logistics materials treated as marketed service evidence rather than independently verified performance.
methodology.case_context: Iran’s China–Central Asia–Iran rail–road logistics adaptation under sustained maritime constraint through September 18, 2026.
methodology.core_problem: The central analytical problem is how nominal gateway and corridor access is converted into reliable delivered supply inside Iran under maritime pressure, border friction, fuel and driver constraints, and inland distribution bottlenecks.
central_claims: Iran’s overland adaptation is becoming a functionally differentiated rail–road architecture rather than a collection of discrete alternative corridors.
Rail and trucking are complementary, not interchangeable, modes of overland resilience.
China–Central Asia regional rail data should not be interpreted as Iran-bound cargo.
TIR reduces customs-transit and guarantee friction but does not imply same-vehicle continuity or zero cargo handling from China to Iran.
The binding issue is capacity conversion rather than route count.
The overland architecture provides selective continuity and threshold delay rather than maritime-scale substitution.
Diversion can create its own constraints by increasing pressure on borders, trucks, drivers, fuel, warehousing, and inland distribution.

analytical_lenses.name: Capacity Conversion
analytical_lenses.description: Assesses how nominal access becomes reliable delivered supply.

analytical_lenses.name: Inland Absorption
analytical_lenses.description: Captures customs, trucks, drivers, fuel, warehousing, roads, and last-mile constraints on Iranian inland logistics.

analytical_lenses.name: Functional Differentiation
analytical_lenses.description: Distinguishes rail and trucking by cargo fit, batch economics, schedule profile, last-mile role, and analytical risk.

analytical_lenses.name: Gateway Conversion
analytical_lenses.description: Separates China-side rail-gateway signals from Iran-bound throughput.

analytical_lenses.name: Land Diversion Paradox
analytical_lenses.description: Identifies how maritime constraint increases land demand and thereby raises congestion, cost, and marginal capacity loss.

analytical_lenses.name: Evidence Grading
analytical_lenses.description: Separates what observed indicators support from what they do not prove.

dimensions.name: Inland Absorption
dimensions.description: Operational availability of nominal Iranian inland capacity across customs, trucks, drivers, fuel, warehousing, roads, and last-mile distribution.
dimensions.observed_pattern: One binding component can cap inland absorption even when other elements retain spare capacity.
dimensions.interpretation: Resilience depends on the weakest inland conversion component.

dimensions.name: Effective Capacity
dimensions.description: End-to-end throughput ceiling across China gateway, transit, Iran gateway, and discounted Iranian inland capacity.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Expansion at one node raises network capacity only when remaining stages can absorb the additional flow.
dimensions.interpretation: Route availability cannot be equated with delivered supply.

dimensions.name: Effective Delivered Supply
dimensions.description: Realized border-entry flow converted into final delivery after inland availability and distribution reliability are applied.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Ainland measures capacity availability; Rdistribution measures reliability conditional on that capacity.
dimensions.interpretation: Border entry does not automatically become delivered supply.

dimensions.name: Rail Layer
dimensions.description: Scheduled, repeatable, containerized, heavier-volume flows through China–Central Asia–Iran alignments.
dimensions.observed_pattern: China–Central Asia rail traffic grew moderately through August 2026; Horgos provides the strongest westbound gateway signal.
dimensions.interpretation: Rail supports repeatability and consolidated movement but should not be read as maritime-equivalent throughput.

dimensions.name: Trucking Layer
dimensions.description: Flexible dispatch, urgent replenishment, smaller-lot access, high-value goods, project cargo, and final-distribution reach.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Operator evidence shows commercial readiness and advertised China–Iran service ranges while also showing transloading in some “direct” services.
dimensions.interpretation: Firm-level road advantage does not imply system-level road substitution.

dimensions.name: TIR Layer
dimensions.description: Standardized customs-transit documentation and guarantee arrangement for sealed transit movements.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Intermodal TIR institutionalization is visible in the broader Central Asian network.
dimensions.interpretation: TIR reduces procedural friction but does not eliminate handoffs or guarantee same-vehicle continuity.

dimensions.name: Land Diversion Paradox
dimensions.description: Maritime capacity decline increases land demand, border and mode load, congestion and cost, which can reduce marginal land effectiveness.
dimensions.observed_pattern: Expanded land traffic produced longer queues, infrastructure strain, higher costs, and reported fuel/driver pressures.
dimensions.interpretation: Diversion can erode the effectiveness of the alternatives intended to absorb maritime shock.

formulas.title: Inland-Absorption Coefficient
formulas.formula: A_inland ≈ min(a_customs, a_trucks, a_drivers, a_fuel, a_warehousing, a_roads, a_last-mile)
formulas.description: Conservative heuristic for the share of nominal Iranian inland logistics capacity that is operationally available.

formulas.title: Effective Capacity
formulas.formula: C_effective = min(C_China gateway, C_transit, C_Iran gateway, C_Iran inland^nom × A_inland)
formulas.description: Heuristic for end-to-end throughput ceiling across gateway, transit, Iranian entry, and inland constraints.

formulas.title: Effective Delivered Supply
formulas.formula: EDS = min(F_entry, C_Iran inland^nom × A_inland) × R_distribution
formulas.description: Heuristic for realized delivered supply after border entry, inland availability, and distribution reliability.

formulas.title: Land Diversion Paradox
formulas.formula: Maritime Capacity ↓ → Land Demand ↑ → Border / Mode Load ↑ → Congestion & Cost ↑ → Marginal Land Effectiveness ↓
formulas.description: Analytical mechanism describing how overland diversion can generate its own congestion and cost constraints.

key_findings: Iran’s overland adaptation has moved beyond route availability toward a structured rail–road architecture.
The overland system remains a resilience system rather than a system-scale replacement for maritime logistics.
China–Central Asia rail data show moderate system growth rather than indiscriminate expansion.
Horgos is the stronger westbound gateway signal, while Alashankou’s cumulative outbound traffic remained below 2025 despite recent recovery.
Rail and trucking are functionally complementary rather than direct substitutes.
TIR should not be equated with a single tractor, driver, or zero cargo handling from China to Iran.
The binding issue is capacity conversion: border processing, trucks, drivers, fuel, warehousing, and domestic distribution determine how much nominal access becomes delivered supply inside Iran.
The overland architecture provides continuity and threshold delay under constraint rather than maritime-scale substitution.
Expanded land diversion can increase congestion and cost, reducing the marginal effectiveness of overland alternatives.
policy_recommendations: Track converted throughput rather than route counts.
Separate regional Central Asia rail data from Iran-bound data.

Assess rail and road by function, cargo fit, frequency, utilization, border dwell, terminal handling, dispatch availability, transload count, fuel and driver conditions, and final-delivery reliability.
Record pricing boundaries before comparing crisis-era logistics quotes.
Treat inland absorption as a leading indicator by monitoring border queues, customs release time, truck and driver availability, fuel access, warehouse conditions, and APRIN utilization.
Code recurring capacity only after repeated movements, realized transit, and downstream release are observed.
